observations.title: Kilauea volcano (United States)
observations.description: The Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (HVO) reported that the eruption within Kilauea?s Kaluapele summit caldera, characterized by incandescence, intermittent spatter, and lava flows from vents along the SW and W margins of Halema`um`u Crater, continued at variable levels during 7-14 October. Incandescence and flaming continued to be visible at the N and S vents during 6-11 October, with periodic spattering at the N vent. Robust volcanic gas plumes rose from both vents in daytime webcam views. Several small lava overflows from a small vent at the base of N vent were observed during 9-10 October. The small vent also intermittently spattered until 2315 on 10 October when it began continuously effusing a small, tube-fed pahoehoe flow. Overnight during 11-12 October moderate-to-strong incandescence was visible at the N vent, at the vent near its base, and at the S vent, while incandescence from the W vent fluctuated, with visibility potentially affected by fog. Intermittent flames and minor spattering associated with gas jetting occurred at all vents, including a short period of sustained spattering at the S vent that began at around 0318 on 12 October. Spattering from the vent at the base of the N vent occurred intermittently. Visible spattering ended at around 0635. Vigorous dome fountaining began at the N vent just before 1130 on 13 October, lasted nearly an hour, and produced a lava flow that traveled about 1 km. This was the longest and most vigorous dome fountain since 30 September. Two other substantial fountain and overflow episodes occurred at 1600-1640 and at 1700-1720. Interspersed between and following these longer events were about 15 smaller events that lasted only a few minutes and produced flows less than 100 m long. Sustained fountaining was followed by gas jetting, often with sprays of spatter produced during drainbacks of lava within the vents. The Volcano Alert Level remained at Watch (the second highest level on a four-level scale) and the Aviation Color Code at Orange (the second highest color on a four-color scale). Source: US Geological Survey Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (HVO)
